implementation_notes: Rails' ActiveModel is the dominant realization and it returns rather than throws: include ActiveModel::Validations, declare the rules with validates, call valid? (a boolean) and read errors - errors.add appends one entry per failed rule, errors.full_messages localises them, and errors.details carries the machine-readable attribute/type pair for an API. ActiveRecord models get the same errors object for free, which is why hand-rolled accumulators are rare in Ruby; dry-validation's Result object is the schema-first alternative outside Rails.
code_sketch:
class BookingRequest
  include ActiveModel::Validations
  attr_accessor :seats, :date

  validates :seats, numericality: { greater_than: 0, less_than_or_equal_to: 20 }
  validates :date, presence: true
end

request.valid?                # => false, every failure recorded
request.errors.details        # => {seats: [{error: :greater_than, value: 0, count: 0}], date: [{error: :blank}]}
request.errors.full_messages  # => ["Seats must be greater than 0", "Date can't be blank"]
pitfalls: valid? clears the previous errors and re-runs every validation, but error entries added with strict: true raise instead of recording - avoid strict mode on an accumulating path.
errors[:seats] returns only the message strings; errors.details is the machine-readable form (attribute, error type, options) that survives i18n.
Calling save/update without checking valid? is the classic silent-failure bug: the call returns false, the record stays unchanged and the errors are ignored.
